Simulation assumptions & research sources — adjust walking and robot speeds

Adjust the scenario

Human 1.20 m/s is a scenario assumption, not a universal measured warehouse speed. The default robot rates use the selected brochure's published maximum speeds: 2.3 m/s empty and 2.0 m/s loaded. These are not necessarily typical operating speeds or guaranteed trip averages. Lower illustrative profiles remain available.

Time assumptions: 6 s to pick one item on either side; 4 s lift (brochure); 4 s lower and 1 s station clearance (assumed). Travel duration = route distance ÷ the relevant speed. The drawing is schematic, using 0.12 m per SVG unit for travel accounting; rack icons are not dimensionally scaled.

What this model includes

Same rack locations, three different SKUs and one picker per side. The manual route is the shortest of the six SKU sequences on the drawn aisle network. The worker collects all items before returning. No extra manual search penalty is added.

Each robot carries one shelf. Available robots retrieve in parallel, wait in assigned staging bays, and enter the shared station in arrival order. Station admission, picking and exit are exclusive. A robot becomes available again after returning and lowering its shelf.

Order ready: all three items are at the station. System reset: the manual worker has returned, or every robot has returned and lowered its shelf. Local reaching, packing, charging, acceleration, detailed intersection control and aisle congestion are excluded. Buffers and dispatch are illustrative, not an exact Geek+ RMS implementation.

Research: Geek+'s P800R sheet specifies empty travel at 2.3 m/s, loaded travel at 2.0 m/s and lifting at 4 s; specifications vary by generation. The official Shelf-to-Person workflow uses fleet dispatch, shelf delivery, operator confirmation and shelf return. Queue-based pod delivery is also described in RMFS research.

04 · SIZING & CAPACITY

Recommended Solution for Demo Distribution Center

Current fleet (FIFO dispatch) vs. queue-aware candidates: up to 32 robots and 6 placed stations within budget. Every candidate sees identical random arrivals at the design rate; KPIs are measured over 60 min after a 10-min warm-up and averaged over 3 seeds.

Ready to evaluate the current layout.

Analyze the layout to see a recommendation supported by actual routes, resource queues and costs.

Model, bottleneck logic and planning checks

Four-neighbor breadth-first search computes shortest paths on the same 1 m grid you edit. Blocked cells include obstacles, restrictions, storage bays, chargers and stations inflated by a 1 m center clearance. Entry, exit and keep-clear aisle markings are traversable. Each bay has a short final docking connector; the simulation includes both end connectors in travel distance.

Each shelf visit requires empty retrieval, a 4 s lift, loaded delivery, a station service slot (pick seconds × lines on that visit), loaded return and a 4 s drop. Visits arrive as a Poisson process at the design rate ÷ hit rate. Robots and station slots are reserved by an event scheduler. The baseline selects the earliest-free robot and nearest station; candidate dispatch considers predicted picking completion. No arbitrary improvement multiplier or machine learning is used.

The first 10 minutes (cold start) are simulated but excluded; KPIs cover the next 60 minutes and are averaged over 3 seeds, with the same seeds for every candidate. Latency includes completed lines only. The analytic capacity ceiling is min(fleet × 3,600 / mean uncongested cycle, stations × 3,600 / pick seconds). It is an optimistic capacity bound, not guaranteed sustained output.

Planning checks: observed throughput ≥ 97% of arrived lines, unfinished work no greater than the modeled in-flight allowance plus 2% of arrivals, at least 10% analytic capacity headroom over the design rate, and enough SKU slots. The in-flight allowance is ceil(arrival rate × average uncongested order lead time). The cheapest configuration passing these checks is proposed; otherwise the best completion count within budget is shown with unmet requirements.

Route overlap flags potential congestion. The model does not simulate inter-robot collision avoidance, charging schedules, acceleration profiles, safety interlocks, SKU replenishment, batching, equipment reliability or production traffic-control software. The original loop simulator remains available below as a separate reference experiment.

05 · ASSUMPTION-BASED BUSINESS CASE

Technical performance meets investment constraints.

All costs are editable illustrative assumptions in USD. They are not Geek+ prices or a quotation. Change assumptions, apply them, then rerun the comparison.

Financial formulas and limitations

Capex = robots × robot cost + stations × station cost + racks × rack cost + integration cost. Annual operating cost = station-operator labor + maintenance (% of capex) + annual energy + annual software.

Manual operators = ceil(average lines per hour / assumed manual productivity). Automated operators = one per proposed picking station. Labor savings = (manual operators − automated operators) × hours/day × working days × hourly cost. Net annual savings = labor savings − maintenance − energy − software. Simple payback = capex / positive net savings; zero or negative savings produce “No positive payback.” First-year net savings / capex is shown as a simple ratio, not an investment return forecast.

Both options must be assessed against the same demand. Where capacity or storage checks fail, savings are explicitly conditional and must not be presented as a feasible business case. Staffing is whole-person, full-shift; taxes, financing, discounting, residual value and inflation are excluded.

How the heuristic engine works · assumptions, routes, and KPI definitions

Actual simulation, transparent simplifications

This mode models a 10-minute, cold-start sample of an 8-hour day. Each order is one line requiring one shelf visit. Deterministic uniform arrivals are scaled by the peak-demand factor. A seeded SKU stream (seed 73129) gives both configurations identical orders. This optimizer sample is separate from the original three-line comparison.

Published specifications: P800R empty 2.3 m/s, loaded 2.0 m/s. The speed allowance scales both; these are ceilings, not guaranteed operating averages. Human walking remains 1.2 m/s in the original mode; optimizer pickers remain at stations.

Assumed parameters: a 64 m one-way loop; 12 shelf bays and 1–3 picking stations; 2 m bay connectors; 2.8 m robot center clearance; 4 s lift and lower; 30 s workstation service per one-line order including handling and confirmation. The original mode retains its 6 s item pick.

Each bay is exclusive. A robot carries one shelf, delivers it, waits through picking, returns the shelf and lowers it. Loaded robots never route through another stored shelf. Robots wait before occupied bays; merges need clearance ahead and behind. The single lane has no overtaking. Acceleration, charging, safety certification and complex intersections are outside this demonstration.

Scheduling, search and measurement

Baseline: oldest available order, first available robot, fixed SKU-to-station assignment. Locked shelves are skipped until returned. Queue-aware alternative: chooses a robot/order pair from the oldest 16 available orders using legal clockwise travel, station reservations and an order-age preference; chooses the station with the lowest reserved-service plus inbound-travel estimate. Same one-way routing rules apply to both.

A local candidate search tests dispatch changes, ± robot capacity, ± station capacity and combinations. Score = completed orders − 0.2 × robots − 0.8 × stations − 0.002 × mean completed-order latency in seconds. These are illustrative preference weights, not financial costs. Candidates completing fewer orders than baseline are rejected. The baseline itself can win. Recommendations are limited to the tested candidates, not a proven global optimum.

Event-derived KPIs: throughput = completed orders ÷ elapsed time; latency = completion − arrival; robot busy time includes assigned travel, service and waiting; station utilization counts picking service only. Travel includes empty and loaded distance. Robot waiting includes blocked lane/merge time. Station idle = available station seconds − service seconds. Backlog includes every arrived, unfinished order.

The engine advances in deterministic 0.25 s steps, with conservative movement at state transitions. Heat intensity uses the same scale in both views: full amber represents at least 60 robot-wait seconds in a 2 m aisle zone. Observed utilization and waiting identify likely constraints; controlled candidate comparisons test the diagnosis. The visuals are schematic, and all gains are calculated model results, not official Geek+ claims.

What is verified, and what is illustrative?

Verified: the specifications above come from the single v6.0 brochure column; the exterior styling takes cues from Geek+’s v6 product image. Illustrative: geometry, wheel and sensor placement, lifting internals, lighting, rack, workstation, motion profile and task sequence. This is an independent presentation model, not an official digital twin, safety model, CAD file or Geek+ control software.

The 49-second sequence (three pick-and-put cycles) uses conservative display speeds, smooth acceleration and a 4-second lift. The platform first closes an illustrative 20 mm contact gap, then lifts the rack 40 mm within its 60 mm stroke. The workstation follows the supplied two-column Geek+ reference image. Its dimensions, rear approach, stopping plane, projector optics, human movement and confirmation sequence are illustrative assumptions, not verified manufacturer docking or safety specifications. The shelf stays behind the front rails; light guides the human and does not pick the product. Picking and return/lowering times are presentation assumptions. This sequence does not calculate or change the KPIs in either warehouse tab. Fleet coordination explanations describe general systems engineering; Geek+ describes RMS as robot scheduling and WES as task logic ↗.

The 3D library is bundled locally. The optional video and source links require internet access. If WebGL 2 is unavailable, the illustrative image and technical panels remain accessible.
